01 · Inception · Spatial context

Receptive Fields and Filter Size

Can one value tell us whether it belongs to a corner, a line, or a larger outline?

A convolution combines values within its local window. Compare three windows at the same position, then click a window to inspect the values inside it.

Input feature map

Same input for every window

Inside the selected window

3 × 3 neighbourhood

Each enlarged cell corresponds to one highlighted input value. Move the window to compare different parts of the pattern.

Why retain 1 × 1? It mixes information across channels at each position without combining neighbouring positions. It can also change the number of channels at relatively low cost.

A single filter size provides one local window size. Parallel paths allow a layer to use several sizes together.

02 · Inception · Parallel feature extraction

Combining Multiple Feature Paths

What if a layer could use a narrow view, a wider view, and a local maximum together?

Begin with a 28 × 28 colour image: its three channels are red, green and blue. Send the same input into parallel branches, then concatenate their output channels.

RGB input28 × 28 × 3

Why a parallel pooling branch? It supplies local maximum responses alongside the learned convolutional responses. Here, stride 1 and padding preserve the grid, so pooling provides another feature path rather than downsampling the whole network.

Inspect learned responses at different object sizes

This trained three-class network follows the same parallel-path idea. The diagram shows the network that produced the maps below.

The 3 × 3 and 5 × 5 paths use four-channel 1 × 1 reductions. Channel reduction is developed in the next section.

Same stem output → four feature paths

Real responses from the trained network. The four displayed maps use one shared colour scale.

The branches supply different local operations. As earlier layers produce more channels, applying large filters to every channel becomes expensive.

03 · Inception · Efficient computation

Reducing the Cost of Large Filters

A layer receives 64 feature channels. Must every 5 × 5 filter process all 64 directly?

An earlier convolution has produced a 28 × 28 × 64 feature tensor. We want 32 output channels. Compare two ways to produce that same output shape.

Step 1 · Establish the cost

Direct 5 × 5 Convolution

Input features28 × 28 × 64
→
32 filters · 5 × 5Each filter spans all 64 channels
→
Output features28 × 28 × 32
One filter contains 64 spatial slices.

Each slice has 25 weights. One bias is added after the contributions from all input channels are combined.

Weights in one filter5 × 5 × 64 = 1,600
Include its bias1,600 + 1 = 1,601
Across 32 filters1,601 × 32 = 51,232

Step 2 · Change what the large filter receives

Channel Reduction with 1 × 1 Filters

A 1 × 1 filter reads all channels at one position and makes one weighted combination. Using 16 such filters converts 64 input channels into 16 output channels while preserving the 28 × 28 grid.

64 channel valuesAt one spatial position
→
16 learned combinations16 filters of size 1 × 1 × 64
→
16 channel valuesAt that same position
Inspect one small channel-mixing example

At one position, four input channels contain 2, 0, 1 and 3. A 1 × 1 filter with weights ½, ¼, 0 and ½ combines them into one value:

½ × 2 + ¼ × 0 + 0 × 1 + ½ × 3 = 2.5

A second filter uses its own weights to produce a second channel. The same filters are applied at every position.

Step 3 · Calculate both layers

1 × 1 Reduction Followed by 5 × 5 Convolution

Input28 × 28 × 64
→
1 × 1 · 16 filters28 × 28 × 16
→
5 × 5 · 32 filters28 × 28 × 32
Reduction layer(1 × 1 × 64 + 1) × 16 = 1,040
Large-filter layer(5 × 5 × 16 + 1) × 32 = 12,832
Both layers together1,040 + 12,832 = 13,872

Same output dimensions; 51,232 → 13,872 parameters. The large filters now process 16 channels instead of 64. The reduction layer adds some work, but saves much more work in the large-filter layer.

The reduction width is a design choice: fewer channels reduce cost, but also restrict how much information can pass through.

Place these reductions before the large filters in a parallel module. The network can then repeat the module without an uncontrolled increase in computation.

04 · Inception · Complete architecture

GoogLeNet: Connected Modules and Classifiers

Follow the complete main path from top to bottom. The nine Inception modules form a deep network; select any module to inspect its parallel branches below.

Additional feedback during training. Two small classifiers ask intermediate features to predict the image class. Their errors provide additional learning signals to earlier layers. During prediction, the network uses only the main classifier.

Every convolution is followed by ReLU. Within a module, stride 1 and padding keep each branch at the same spatial size.

From Final Feature Maps to a Class Prediction

Global average pooling turns each final feature map into one value. A single linear classifier combines those values into class scores, and softmax produces class probabilities.

Final feature maps7 × 7 × 1024
→
Average each map1024 values
→
One linear classifier1000 scores → probabilities

The large stack of fully connected layers is replaced by spatial averaging and one final linear layer. Dropout is applied before the linear layer during training.

ResNet · Learning with greater depth

Preserving a Useful Representation

More parameters provide more possible transformations. The next experiment asks how easily training can turn those possibilities into useful predictions.

05 · ResNet · The training problem

Depth and Training Performance

How can a shallow network learn better when a deeper network has more parameters?

Train two networks to recognize the same handwritten digits. Compare their training loss first, then inspect their predictions on the same held-out images.

Capacity and successful training are different. More layers add possible transformations, but also add transformations that must learn to work together. An early layer's update depends on the layers after it, which are also changing during training. A shorter chain can reach a useful solution more easily.

Higher training loss means the deeper network has not fitted the training examples as well. This is an optimization difficulty. It is not explained by overfitting alone.

06 · ResNet · Constructing the solution

Preserving a Feature Through Additional Layers

An early convolution has found a useful edge. Can later blocks preserve it while learning what to change?

Follow One Edge Response

Apply successive transformations to the same edge map. Keep the original visible while inspecting the output of each step.

This controlled example uses local averaging and scaling, making changes to a response easy to inspect. A changed feature is not automatically a worse feature; the training curves establish the performance difference.

In the plain path, all information must pass through the learned transformations. Introduce a direct path around a block so the input can also reach its output without being transformed by that block.

Input Plus a Correction

Input x

Correction F(x)

Sum x + F(x)

y = x + F(x)

Set the correction to inspect the addition. Positive corrections increase responses; negative corrections decrease them. The maps share a fixed colour scale.

A plain block must learn the complete output. A residual block can preserve its input directly and learn how to modify it. At the addition, a zero residual gives the input back. The following ReLU preserves nonnegative input features.

How the shortcut also helps the backward path
Earlier features
←
Direct shortcut routeFeedback through the addition
←
Later features

At the addition, learning signals can return through both the learned branch and the direct path. This gives the block an additional route for updating earlier features. ReLU and the other operations still affect the gradients.

07 · ResNet · Testing the change

Training with Residual Connections

Now add shortcuts to the deep network. Its learned layers, parameter count, initialization and training batches match the deep plain network. Compare the complete training runs.

Experimental setup and measured residual maps

MNIST digit classification: 2400 training images and 600 separate test images. Adam, learning rate 0.001, batch size 120, 18 epochs, seed 19. Each block has two padded 3 × 3 convolutions with eight channels. ReLU follows the first convolution and the block output. The models in this experiment use no batch normalization.

The shallow model has one block; both deep models have twelve. A stem convolution, 2 × 2 pooling and a final linear classifier complete each network. The depth labels count convolutions and the final linear layer.

Negative ← zero → positive · shared scale

Actual first-block activations of the trained residual digit network. The input, correction, sum and post-ReLU output are shown separately.

The shortcut provides a useful way to express the computation. The measured loss and predictions show what this change achieves during training.

08 · ResNet · Complete architecture

ResNet-18: Connected Residual Stages

Follow the main path through four stages. Each stage contains two residual blocks. Select a block to inspect both its main path and its shortcut.

RGB input224 × 224 × 3
→
7 × 7 conv · 64Stride 2, padding 3 · BN · ReLU112 × 112 × 64
→
3 × 3 max poolStride 2, padding 1 · 56 × 56 × 64
↓
↓
Global average pooling7 × 7 × 512 → 512 values
→
Linear + softmax1000 classes

BN denotes batch normalization, which normalizes and rescales channels. The main path has one stem convolution, sixteen block convolutions and one final linear layer: eighteen learned layers.

Matching Shapes at a Stage Boundary

The main path halves the image size and doubles the channels. Can its output still be added to the original input?

Main path output28 × 28 × 128
+

A learned 1 × 1 projection sets the shortcut to 128 channels. Stride 2 halves its spatial size. Batch normalization follows the projection.

Two Designs, Two Merge Operations

Inception

Extract features through parallel paths. Use channel reduction to control cost. Concatenate the channel groups.

ResNet

Retain a direct path for the input. Learn a residual change. Add corresponding values after matching the shapes.
